notes:
Task and constraints: Count integers with unique digits using lengths from zero through n.
Idea: Use permutations to count valid positive numbers of each digit length.
Technique and why it applies: nPr lazily extends a factorial table and computes 9P(i); the answer adds one for zero and nine choices for the leading digit times each permutation count.
Invariant: A d-digit positive number has nine choices for its first digit and decreasing unused choices thereafter.
Edge cases: For n=0 the sum is empty and returns one; standard problem constraints keep n small.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) storage for factorial values, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Count numbers with unique digits among values having at most n digits.
Idea: Accumulate the number of valid numbers at each additional digit length.
Technique and why it applies: cnt begins at one and is multiplied by 9-i for each additional position; result sums these counts before multiplying by nine for the first digit.
Invariant: The first digit has nine choices, and each later digit has one fewer available choice.
Edge cases: n=0 returns one directly; for the usual constraint range the factors remain valid.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) extra space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two jugs can measure exactly targetCapacity litres using filling, emptying, and pouring.
Idea: Handle direct capacity cases, then explore reduced capacity differences with a stack and visited set.
Technique and why it applies: The method checks target against either jug and their sum, orders capacities, then repeatedly subtracts the smaller capacity and explores derived differences.
Invariant: The visited set avoids processing the same difference state repeatedly.
Edge cases: Targets larger than total capacity fail immediately; the state exploration is more complicated than the standard gcd criterion and should be tested carefully.
Complexity: Time and space depend on visited difference states and can grow with capacities. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether two jug capacities can measure exactly z litres.
Idea: Use the gcd criterion after checking that the total capacity is sufficient.
Technique and why it applies: Euclid's algorithm computes gcd(x,y); the target is measurable exactly when it is zero or no larger than x+y and divisible by the gcd.
Invariant: All integer combinations of jug capacities are multiples of their gcd, and the capacity bound is necessary.
Edge cases: z=0 succeeds; if x and y are both zero, z=0 short-circuits before modulo by gcd(0,0).
Complexity: O(log max(x,y)) time and O(1) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Determine whether num is a perfect square without using a square-root operation.
Idea: Binary-search candidate roots between two and num//2.
Technique and why it applies: The loop squares the midpoint and narrows the search interval based on comparison with num.
Invariant: The search interval retains any possible integer square root.
Edge cases: num=1 is handled directly, but the code compares mid*mid with undefined variable n rather than num, causing a NameError; it also prints mid.
Complexity: Intended O(log num) time and O(1) space, but the implementation is incorrect as written. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return a largest subset in which every pair is divisible one way by the other.
Idea: Sort values and use dynamic programming to track the longest divisible chain ending at each index.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i] stores chain length and hashh[i] stores its predecessor; each earlier j is checked for divisibility before extending the chain.
Invariant: Sorting means if nums[i] is divisible by nums[j], the smaller value can precede the larger one.
Edge cases: The code assumes positive nonzero values; zero would cause modulo by zero. It mutates nums by sorting.
Complexity: O(n^2) time and O(n) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find a largest subset where every pair is divisible in one direction.
Idea: Sort values and build a longest divisible chain ending at each index.
Technique and why it applies: dp tracks chain lengths and prev stores predecessor indices; a divisible earlier value can extend the chain before the best endpoint is reconstructed.
Invariant: Each predecessor chain is a valid divisible subset because sorted positive values preserve divisibility order.
Edge cases: Empty input returns an empty list; nums is sorted in place.
Complexity: O(n^2) time and O(n) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Add two signed integers without using the arithmetic addition operator.
Idea: Use XOR for partial sums and AND-shift for carries under a 32-bit mask.
Technique and why it applies: The code normalizes inputs to 32-bit signed representations, repeatedly computes carry=a&b and partial sum a^b, then shifts the carry left until it becomes zero.
Invariant: XOR adds bits without carry; the shifted AND identifies carry bits for the next iteration.
Edge cases: The mask and sign-bit handling are tailored to 32-bit signed integers, as required by the problem.
Complexity: O(1) time and space under fixed 32-bit bounds; matches labels.

Task and constraints: Compute a^b modulo 1337 where b is represented as decimal digits.
Idea: Process exponent digits left to right using modular exponentiation identities.
Technique and why it applies: For each digit, raise the accumulated result to the tenth power and multiply by a raised to the current digit, reducing modulo 1337.
Invariant: Appending a decimal digit transforms exponent e into 10e+digit, yielding the update rule.
Edge cases: The empty exponent list would return one, though constraints provide a digit list.
Complexity: Time is O(len(b)) with bounded modular powers and O(1) auxiliary space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Evaluate a raised to the large decimal exponent b modulo 1337.
Idea: Use binary modular exponentiation inside a digit-by-digit exponent fold.
Technique and why it applies: myPow repeatedly squares x and multiplies result for set bits; the outer loop applies result^10 times a^digit modulo 1337.
Invariant: Each processed digit extends the exponent by one decimal place.
Edge cases: Modulo operations keep intermediate values bounded; the code assumes b is a valid digit list.
Complexity: O(len(b)) time with constant-size modular arithmetic and O(1) extra space, consistent with the space label.

Task and constraints: Return k pairs with the smallest sums from two sorted arrays.
Idea: Maintain a max-heap of the best candidate pairs seen so far.
Technique and why it applies: The heap stores negative sums and pair values; once full, a candidate worse than the heap maximum causes the inner loop to break, otherwise it replaces the current worst pair.
Invariant: Because both arrays are sorted, later j values in a row have nondecreasing sums.
Edge cases: The method scans only the first k values from each array and returns heap contents unsorted; empty arrays yield no pairs.
Complexity: Worst-case time can be O(k^2 log k) and heap space O(k). No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the k pairs with smallest sums from two arrays.
Idea: Generate the Cartesian product and select its k smallest entries by sum.
Technique and why it applies: itertools.product enumerates every pair; heapq.nsmallest selects k using the sum of each pair as its key.
Invariant: The selection is correct because it ranks all possible pairs by their combined values.
Edge cases: If k exceeds the number of possible pairs, all pairs are returned; full product generation can be costly.
Complexity: Time is roughly O(mn log k) and auxiliary storage depends on nsmallest's selection, typically O(k) beyond iteration. No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find k pairs with smallest sums from two sorted arrays.
Idea: Use a min-heap to expand neighboring pair indices from the smallest available pair.
Technique and why it applies: The heap begins at (0,0); after popping (i,j), it pushes (i,j+1) and, when j=0, also (i+1,0), avoiding duplicate frontier expansion.
Invariant: Sorted arrays ensure moving right or down cannot decrease pair sums.
Edge cases: If one array is longer, the method swaps arrays recursively and swaps pair coordinates back. It stops after k pairs or heap exhaustion.
Complexity: O(k log min(m,n)) typical heap work and O(min(m,n)) heap space, plus output. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum amount of money needed to guarantee guessing a number from one through n.
Idea: Use memoized minimax recursion over intervals and choose a guess minimizing worst-case cost.
Technique and why it applies: For each interval [l,r], dp tries choices from midpoint through r and adds the guess value to the worse of the left and right interval costs.
Invariant: The recurrence models paying for a wrong guess and then continuing in the remaining interval.
Edge cases: lru_cache is referenced without an import; restricting guesses to the upper half should be checked against the full minimax recurrence.
Complexity: Memoized interval DP uses O(n^2) states and up to O(n) choices per state, or O(n^3) time. No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum guaranteed cost for the number guessing game.
Idea: Use interval dynamic programming and minimize each possible guess's worst-case remaining cost.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i][j] stores the minimum cost for an interval; each k adds its guess value to max(left-subinterval cost, right-subinterval cost).
Invariant: The state is optimal when it minimizes the worst of the two possible remaining intervals.
Edge cases: Intervals of length zero or one retain zero cost from initialization.
Complexity: O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum guaranteed cost to guess a number from one through n.
Idea: Fill interval DP states by increasing right endpoint and minimize over guesses.
Technique and why it applies: For every interval [i,j), the code tests each guess k and adds k+1 to the maximum cost of the two resulting subintervals.
Invariant: Each state represents the cheapest guess whose worst-case continuation is minimized.
Edge cases: Short intervals remain zero from initialization; the half-open indexing keeps subproblems consistent.
Complexity: O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest subsequence whose adjacent differences alternate in sign.
Idea: Track best wiggle lengths ending with an upward or downward move.
Technique and why it applies: When nums[i] rises, positive becomes negative+1; when it falls, negative becomes positive+1.
Invariant: An up-step extends a sequence ending down, and a down-step extends one ending up.
Edge cases: Equal adjacent values change neither state; arrays shorter than two return their length.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space, as stated in comments. No labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the longest wiggle subsequence, where adjacent differences alternate direction.
Idea: Track the current length and whether the last accepted step was up or down.
Technique and why it applies: The scan increments length only when a rise follows no prior direction or a down direction, and vice versa for a fall.
Invariant: Each accepted direction change extends the longest wiggle subsequence seen so far.
Edge cases: Equal values are ignored; arrays shorter than two return their length.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space, matching labels.

Task and constraints: Count ordered sequences of numbers from nums that sum to target.
Idea: Use dynamic programming by total, adding ways for every final number choice.
Technique and why it applies: dp[0]=1; for each total i, every num no larger than i contributes dp[i-num] ways.
Invariant: dp[i] counts ordered combinations because each possible last number is considered for each total.
Edge cases: Positive nums are assumed; target zero returns one empty sequence.
Complexity: O(target·len(nums)) time and O(target) space. No author labels supplied.

Task and constraints: Count ordered combinations of nums that sum to target.
Idea: Build a one-dimensional DP and sort nums so inner loops can stop early.
Technique and why it applies: For each total i, every value no larger than i contributes dp[i-nums[j]]; larger values break the sorted scan.
Invariant: dp[i] accumulates ways by choosing each value as the final element, so order matters.
Edge cases: Sorting mutates nums; positive candidates make the early break valid.
Complexity: O(target·len(nums)) time and O(target) space, matching the space label.
